learning_objective: 🎯 Become a data detective! Learn how to collect, organize, and visually present large sets of messy numbers so they actually make sense.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Data is everywhere. 'Primary Data' is information you collect yourself (like counting the number of fans in your school). 'Secondary Data' is information you get from somewhere else (like looking up internet temperatures).

Looking at 100 random test scores is confusing. We organize them using a 'Frequency Distribution Table'. We group numbers into 'Class Intervals' (like 0-10, 10-20) and use Tally Marks to count how many fall into each group.

A Bar Graph uses separate rectangular bars to show data for categories. A Histogram looks similar but the bars touch each other—it is specifically used for continuous class intervals (like heights from 140cm to 150cm).

fun_activity.title: 👟 The Shoe Size Survey
fun_activity.instructions: Ask 15 people in your family or neighborhood for their shoe size. Create a Tally Mark table grouping them (e.g., sizes 4-6, 7-9, 10-12). Which group has the highest 'Frequency'?

exam_tips: 📌 The biggest difference between a Bar Graph and a Histogram: Bar graphs have gaps between the bars (for categories), Histograms have NO gaps (for continuous numbers).
📌 To find the 'Class Mark' (the exact middle of a class interval), use the formula: $\frac{\text{Lower Limit} + \text{Upper Limit}}{2}$.
📌 In a continuous class interval like '10-20', the number 20 is NOT counted in that group. It is counted in the next group, '20-30'.
quick_recap: ⭐ Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, and analyzing numerical data.
⭐ Frequency distribution tables simplify raw data using intervals and tally marks.
⭐ Visual graphs like Histograms and Bar Graphs make large datasets instantly understandable.
